page.title: SpringSaLaD Application
page.introduction: A SpringSaLaD application adds spatial detail to the Sites and Links of a Molecule, and defines and runs simulations with the Langevin solver. It is created over an existing rule-based physiology - see Introduction to SpringSaLaD Modeling for what the framework represents.
page.appearance:
When using SpringSaLaD Applications, it is important to be aware that:
The Langevin solver can be used with any Rule-based model that obeys the limitations described below.
The Langevin solver performs a stochastic simulation, so simulation results will vary by run.
A very strict geometry is required.
The complexity of calculations makes it practical only for a small number of particles.
Parameter overrides and parameter scans are not supported. Repeat runs are asked for as Multiple Runs on the simulation instead.
Using a SpringSaLaD application has the following limitations:
The model must have exactly 3 structures: 2 compartments named "Intracellular" and "Extracellular", separated by a membrane named "Membrane". The names are not conventions - the solver input is written by looking them up.
Every site needs attributes the rest of VCell has no use for: a radius, a diffusion rate, a position, a colour, and links to the sites it is bound to.
The reaction rules are strictly categorized and must obey several syntax restrictions.
page.operations:
Creating the application. Right-click Applications in the model tree and choose New Application > SpringSaLaD. Unlike other spatial applications, it does not ask for a geometry: it builds one, a 3D analytic geometry of two subdomains, and maps all three structures into it.
The geometry it builds. A 100 nm cube with the membrane 90 nm up, written as two expressions on the Geometry Definition tab:
Intracellular = (z < 0.09) - everything below the membrane. The value is in microns, and the form matters: the solver input writer parses this expression and needs it to be exactly "z < number".
Extracellular = 1.0 - everything else.
To change the size of the box, press Edit Domain... and set the extent, then move the membrane by editing the Intracellular expression to match. The two are independent: the extent says how tall the box is, the expression says where inside it the membrane sits. A box 0.4 um tall with Intracellular = (z < 0.2) gives 200 nm of cytosol and 200 nm outside.
Specifications. Three tabs, of which two behave differently here:
Molecular Structures - the site geometry: where each site sits, how big it is, how fast it diffuses, what colour it is drawn in, and which sites are sprung together.
Reaction - which of the five SpringSaLaD subtypes VCell has recognised each rule as, and whether it is enabled in this application.
Species - initial conditions. Switch the table to Number of Particles if you want to say "20 molecules" rather than a concentration; SpringSaLaD counts particles.
Solver options. On a simulation, press Edit and open the Solver tab. The integrator is LangevinNoVis, and the Langevin Options Panel below it carries everything the simulation needs that a deterministic one does not:
Time Step (Default) - the integration step. Values in the 1-10 ns range are usual.
Spring Interval - the step used for spring relaxation, normally left alone.
Image Interval - how often a full snapshot of every particle position is stored. This is what the 3D Trajectory viewer plays back, and it is separate from the output interval that governs the counts.
Output Interval - how often the counters are sampled.
Partitions number, X, Y and Z - space is divided into boxes so that collision detection only has to compare neighbours. There is one rule to respect: a partition must be larger than the diameter of the largest site. With a 100 nm box and 10 partitions the cells are 10 nm across, which is fine for sites of radius 2 nm and not fine for sites of radius 6.
Single Trajectory or Multiple Runs - one run, or N independent runs whose average and spread are the result. Total Num. Of Jobs is N; Num. Concurrent Jobs is how many run at once.
Set a seed to Langevin random number generator - fix the seed and a run is reproducible, which is the only way to compare two versions of a model change by change.
Running it. A SpringSaLaD simulation runs on the server like any other, and also runs locally through Native Quick Run, which uses the Langevin solver bundled with the client and saves nothing to the database - useful for a short run while the model is still being built.
